sentences: The bookseller owns a travel book store in a city neighbourhood.
Divorced from his wife who left him for another man (who resembles a famous actor), he shares a flat with his flatmate, a flaky and sloppy man.
One day, a famous actress enters the shop and buys a book.
Shortly after she leaves, the bookseller goes to buy his colleague a juice, but bumps into the actress while rounding a street corner, spilling it on her.
He takes her to his flat across the street so she can change.
When leaving, she impulsively kisses him.
The actress later invites the bookseller to visit her at her hotel.
There, he is mistaken for a reporter and ushered into a press event for her new film.
When asked, the bookseller says he writes for a magazine.
The actress asks to be the bookseller's date at his sister's birthday party later that evening.
Though his friends and family are surprised, she gets on well with everyone and enjoys herself.
Later, the two enter a private neighbourhood park, where the actress again kisses the bookseller.
At a restaurant, the bookseller and the actress overhear a party of men at a nearby table discussing her, first praising and then disparaging her and equating actresses to prostitutes.
He confronts them, then she introduces herself and calmly insults the stunned men.
The actress invites the bookseller to her hotel room, but after discovering that her movie star boyfriend has unexpectedly arrived from abroad, he leaves.
Over the next six months, the bookseller's friends arrange a series of dates for him, but the bookseller, heartsick over the actress, is uninterested in another relationship.
One day, the distraught actress appears at the bookseller's doorstep, needing to hide due to a tabloid scandal.
She apologises about her boyfriend and says their relationship is over.
They discover shared interests, and discuss the bookseller's print of a painter's 1950 painting.
The actress says it shows "how love should be" and that "happiness isn't happiness without a violin-playing goat" as depicted in the painting.
They have sex that night.
The next morning paparazzi, inadvertently tipped off by the flatmate, besiege the house and take photos of the bookseller, the actress, and a half-dressed flatmate at the front door.
Furious, she blames the bookseller and leaves.
Several seasons pass, and the bookseller remains miserable.
When he discovers that the actress is back in the city making a film based on a novel, something he had suggested, he visits the set unannounced.
She asks him to wait until the shooting is done, but he leaves when overhearing her being dismissive about him to another actor.
The actress comes to the bookshop the next day, bringing a wrapped gift.
The bookseller says he overheard what she said about him to her co-star.
The actress explains that she was merely trying to keep her personal life private.
She proclaims that she loves him, and pleads to rekindle their relationship.
The bookseller refuses, explaining that he would not recover if she left him again.
The bookseller meets his friends and sister at a restaurant with the actress's partly opened gift: the painter's original painting.
They halfheartedly support his decision about the actress until the flatmate arrives and calls him a "daft prick".
The bookseller admits his mistake, and everyone races across the city to find the actress, who is holding a press conference at a hotel.
They arrive just as her publicist, in answer to a question about how long the actress will stay in the country, announces that the actress is taking a year off and is leaving the country that night.
A reporter asks about the embarrassing photographs taken at the bookseller's flat, and the actress says they are just friends.
The bookseller, again portraying a reporter from the magazine, asks her if she would consider being more than friends if he begs her forgiveness.
She says she would, then requests a reporter to repeat his question, "How long are you intending to stay here in the country?"
Smiling, she answers "Indefinitely".
The actress and the bookseller marry, their wedding cake featuring the violin-playing goat from the painting.
An aspiring journalist has recently graduated from university.
Despite her lack of knowledge of the fashion industry, she is hired as a junior personal assistant to the cruel editor-in-chief of a magazine in the city.
The heroine resolves to tolerate the editor-in-chief's abusive treatment until she can use her connections from the magazine to find a journalism-focused job.
The heroine fits in poorly with her superficial, fashion-forward co-workers, particularly the editor-in-chief's senior assistant, and struggles to meet the editor-in-chief's irrational demands.
After she fails to arrange for the editor-in-chief to be flown back from another city during a hurricane, she is berated.
She then approaches the magazine's art director for advice, and he helps her select stylish clothes to fit the extremely fashion-conscious workplace.
Noticing the heroine's increased commitment to the job, the editor-in-chief delegates more important tasks to her.
The heroine soon outperforms the senior assistant, who yearns to attend fashion week as the editor-in-chief's assistant.
In preparation for the event, the senior assistant follows extreme diets that endanger her health.
When the senior assistant arrives to work sick and forgets the names of important guests at a charity benefit, the heroine steps in to save the editor-in-chief from embarrassment.
The editor-in-chief subsequently selects the heroine to accompany her to fashion week.
The senior assistant is horrified that the heroine accepted the editor-in-chief's offer.
After the heroine snaps at her boyfriend, he breaks up with her, disappointed that she has become one of the shallow, egotistical women she once ridiculed.
At fashion week, the heroine learns that the editor-in-chief's husband has filed for divorce.
Later that night, the art director tells the heroine that he has accepted a job as creative director for a rising designer.

The heroine spends the night with an attractive writer, who tells her that a rival editor (the editor-in-chief's counterpart as editor-in-chief at another edition of the magazine) is being prepared to replace the editor-in-chief.
The heroine attempts to warn the editor-in-chief, who dismisses her.

At a luncheon, the editor-in-chief announces the rival editor as the designer's new creative director and later reveals that she already knew of the scheme to replace her and sacrificed the art director's ambitions to preserve her own job.
The heroine is repulsed by the editor-in-chief's betrayal of her friend, but the editor-in-chief points out that the heroine did the same thing to the senior assistant.
Afraid to become the type of person the editor-in-chief is, the heroine storms off.
When the editor-in-chief tries calling her, the heroine tosses her phone into a fountain.
Back in the city, the heroine meets up with her ex-boyfriend, who tells her he has a new job as a sous-chef in another city, and they agree to keep in touch.
The same day, the heroine has an interview at a newspaper.

The editor recounts that when he called the magazine for a reference, the editor-in-chief told him that the heroine was the biggest disappointment she had ever had as an assistant and that he would be an idiot not to hire her.
After getting the job, the heroine calls the senior assistant and offers her the clothes she obtained on the trip.
While walking past the magazine's office building, the heroine sees the editor-in-chief and waves at her.
The editor-in-chief does not acknowledge her but smiles to herself once seated in her car.
A university sorority president is taken to a restaurant by her boyfriend.
She expects a proposal, but he breaks up with her instead.
Intending to become a successful senator, he believes the heroine is not "serious" enough for that life.
He tells her that his family has five generations of senators and that his brother, a student at a law school, is engaged to a woman from a prominent family.
The heroine assumes she can win the ex-boyfriend back by achieving the same things.
After months of studying, the heroine scores a near-perfect 179 on the entrance exam.
With that and her 4.0 GPA, she is accepted to a law school, which the ex-boyfriend will also attend.
During the first semester, the heroine discovers that her personality completely contrasts with those of her distrusting classmates.
The heroine learns of the ex-boyfriend's engagement to his previous girlfriend, and befriends a local manicurist.
Later, as the heroine tells the ex-boyfriend she intends to apply for one of her professor's internships, he says she is not smart enough.
Realizing that the ex-boyfriend will neither take her back nor take her seriously, the heroine determines to demonstrate her understanding of the subject.
The following semester, the school's most respected teacher hires some first-year interns, including the heroine, the ex-boyfriend, and his fiancée, to assist in a high-profile case.
It involves a prominent fitness instructor, one of the heroine's role models and a fellow alumna of her sorority.
Accused of murdering her husband, the fitness instructor is unwilling to publicly reveal her alibi.
However, the fitness instructor tells the heroine in confidence she was secretly having liposuction at the time, which the heroine promises not to disclose.
The fiancée gains new respect for the heroine when she refuses to betray the fitness instructor and divulge the alibi to the professor.
The professor's junior partner recognizes the heroine's potential.
The professor attempts to seduce the heroine, who assumes that is why he recruited her.
She briefly quits in disgust and tells the junior partner what happened.

After learning of the professor's behavior, the fitness instructor replaces him with the heroine under the junior partner's guidance, as law students may act in court under the supervision of a licensed attorney.

While cross-examining the fitness instructor's stepdaughter, the heroine eventually discovers a significant inconsistency in her story: the stepdaughter testified she was home during her father's murder but did not hear the gunshot because she was in the shower after getting her hair permed that morning.
The heroine explains washing permed hair within the first 24 hours would deactivate the ammonium thioglycolate, pointing out the stepdaughter's curls are still intact.
The stepdaughter admits her frustration at having a stepmother her own age, inadvertently confessing she shot her father after mistaking him for the fitness instructor.
With the fitness instructor exonerated, the media hail the heroine's involvement.
The ex-boyfriend asks the heroine to take him back since she has proven herself, but she rejects him, realizing he is shallow and a "complete bonehead".
However, she and the fiancée become best friends, especially after the fiancée dumps the ex-boyfriend.
The heroine gives the graduation speech two years later, while the ex-boyfriend graduates with no honors, job offers, or girlfriend.
The junior partner has started his law firm, with plans to propose to the heroine later that night.

A freelance voice actor lives in the city and is a devoted father to his three children—a fourteen-year-old, a twelve-year-old, and a five-year-old—though his workaholic wife considers him immature and unreliable.

After quitting a job following a disagreement over a morally questionable script, the father returns home to throw his son a chaotic birthday party, despite the mother's objections due to the son's declining grades.
The mother arrives home early to break up the party and, in the ensuing argument, tells the father she wants a divorce.

Due to the father's unemployed and homeless status, the mother is granted sole custody of the children, with the father having visitation rights every Saturday; shared custody is contingent upon the father finding a steady job and suitable residence within three months.
The father secures an apartment and a job as a shipping clerk at a television station.

After learning that the mother is looking to hire a housekeeper, the father secretly alters her classified ad form, then calls her using his voice acting skills to pose as a series of undesirable applicants before calling under an assumed name (a surname he derives from a newspaper headline) as an elderly nanny with strong credentials.
Impressed, the mother invites the nanny for an interview.
The father's makeup artist brother and the brother's domestic partner help the father appear as an old woman through the use of makeup and prosthetics.
The mother hires the nanny following a successful interview.
The kids initially struggle under her authority, but eventually come around and thrive, while the mother becomes more easygoing and closer with the kids.
The father further improves himself as well, becoming more responsible, learning several household skills, and earning the mother's respect.
However, the mother puts more trust in the nanny than in the father, and cannot bring herself to dismiss her.
The mother also begins dating an old friend, much to the father's chagrin.
One night, after the two older children discover the father standing while urinating, he reveals the truth; they agree to keep his secret so that they can continue spending time with him.
One day, the station's CEO sees the father playing with props on the set of a recently cancelled children's show.
Impressed by his voice acting, humor, and imagination, the CEO invites the father to dinner to discuss plans for a new show.
The meeting turns out to be at the same place and time as a planned birthday dinner for the mother, to which the nanny is invited.
The father spends the night changing in and out of the nanny costume to attend both events.
Becoming intoxicated, the father accidentally returns to the CEO in costume, but quickly explains himself by claiming that the nanny is his idea for the new show's host.
After learning of the boyfriend's pepper allergy, the father sneaks into the kitchen and seasons the boyfriend's jambalaya with powdered cayenne.
When the boyfriend begins choking, the guilt-ridden father administers the anti-choking maneuver, accidentally causing the prosthetic mask to slip off and expose his identity.
The horrified mother leaves with the children.

At their next custody hearing, the father points out that he has met the judge's requirements ahead of schedule, then explains that his actions were done out of love for his children and begs to still be allowed to see them.

Disturbed by the father's behavior, the judge grants the mother full custody of the children, only granting the father supervised visitation rights every Saturday, and suggests that the father undergo psychological counseling.
Without the nanny, the mother and the kids become miserable, acknowledging how much "she" improved their lives.
They then discover that the father, as the nanny, is hosting the new children's show, which becomes a nationwide hit.
The mother visits the father on set and admits that things were better when he was involved with the family.
She arranges joint custody, allowing the father to take the children daily after school.

As the father leaves for the day with the children, the mother watches an episode of the show in which the nanny answers a letter from a young girl whose parents recently separated, and assures the girl that no matter what arrangements families have, love will prevail.
A thirteen-year-old boy tries to impress a girl by going on a carnival ride but is rejected as he is too short.
Dejected, he inserts a coin into an antique fortune-teller machine, and makes a wish to be "big".
It dispenses a card stating "Your wish is granted," but the boy notices the machine has been unplugged the entire time.
The next morning, the boy discovers that he has grown into an adult overnight.
Deducing that the fortune-teller machine can actually make wishes come true, he tries to locate the machine, but finds that the carnival has moved on.
Returning home, he desperately tries to explain his predicament to his mother, who panics and chases him from the house thinking he is a stranger who has kidnapped her son.
He then finds his best friend at his school and convinces him of his identity by reciting a song that only they know.

With his best friend's help, the boy learns that it will take at least six weeks to find the fortune-teller machine again, so the boy rents a room in a flophouse in the city and gets a job as a data entry clerk at a toy company.
The boy meets the company's owner at a toy store, and impresses him with his insight into current toys and his child-like enthusiasm.
They use the store's walking piano to play duets, and the owner invites the boy to a massive marketing campaign pitch meeting with senior executives.

Unimpressed with the toy being pitched, the boy shocks and challenges the executives with a simple declaration that the toy is not fun, and while his follow-up suggestions invigorate the team for new ideas, he earns the animosity of the pitch's leader.
Meanwhile, the pleased owner promotes the boy to Vice President of Product Development.
He soon attracts the attention of a fellow executive, and a romance begins to develop, much to the dismay of her former boyfriend, the pitch's leader.
The boy becomes increasingly entwined in his adult life by spending time with the woman, mingling with her friends, and entering into a steady relationship with her.
His ideas become valuable assets to the toy company; however, he begins to forget what it is like to be a child, and his tight schedule rarely allows him to spend time with his best friend.
The owner asks the boy to come up with proposals for a new line of toys.
He is intimidated by the need to formulate the business aspects of the proposal, but the woman says that she will handle the business end while he comes up with the ideas.
Nevertheless, he feels pressured and longs for his old life.
When he expresses doubts to the woman and attempts to explain that he is a child, she interprets this as fear of commitment on his part and dismisses his explanation.
The boy learns from his best friend that the fortune-teller machine is now at a park, and he leaves in the middle of his presentation to the owner and the other executives.
The woman follows and encounters his best friend, who tells her where the boy went.
At the park, the boy finds the machine, unplugs it, and makes a wish to become a child again.
The woman confronts him for running off, but upon seeing the machine and the fortune, she realizes that he was telling the truth and becomes despondent that their relationship will end.
The boy is grateful for their time together and suggests she use the machine to turn herself into a little girl.
The woman declines, but offers to drive the boy back home.
After sharing an emotional goodbye with the woman, the boy transforms into a child again before reuniting with his family and best friend.
The hero is an asocial ogre who loves the solitude of his swamp and enjoys fending off mobs and intruders.
One day, his life is interrupted after he inadvertently saves a talkative donkey from some soldiers, prompting the donkey to forcibly stay with him.
The donkey is one of many fairy tale creatures that are being exiled by a dwarfish lord to beautify his land.
However, the creatures inadvertently end up in the swamp.

Angered by the intrusion, the ogre resolves to visit the lord and demand that he move the creatures elsewhere, reluctantly allowing the donkey to accompany him as he is the only one who knows where the lord's kingdom is.
Meanwhile, the lord asks a magic mirror if he has the most perfect kingdom; the mirror tells him he is not a king and would need to marry a princess in order to become one.
Presented with three options, the lord chooses a princess who is imprisoned in a castle guarded by a dragon.
Unwilling to rescue the princess himself, he organizes a tournament, the winner receiving the "privilege" of rescuing her on his behalf.

When the lord sees the ogre and the donkey in his castle, he announces that whoever kills the ogre will win the tournament; however, the ogre and the donkey defeat the lord's knights with relative ease.
Amused, the lord proclaims the ogre his champion, and agrees to relocate the fairy tale creatures in exchange for the ogre rescuing the princess.
The ogre and the donkey travel to the castle and the dragon attacks them.

The ogre locates the princess, who is bewildered by his lack of romanticism; they flee the castle after rescuing the donkey from the dragon, who is revealed to be female and has fallen in love with him.

When the ogre removes his helmet and reveals he is an ogre, the princess stubbornly refuses to go to the kingdom, demanding the lord arrive in person to save her, but the ogre carries the princess against her will.
That night, after setting up camp, and with the princess alone in a cave, the ogre admits to the donkey that he is asocial because he grew frustrated over being constantly judged for his appearance.
The princess overhears this and becomes kinder to the ogre.
The next day, an outlaw and his band of men harass the three, but the princess easily defeats them in physical combat.
The ogre becomes impressed with the princess, and they begin to fall in love.
When the trio nears the kingdom, the princess takes shelter in a windmill for the evening.
The donkey enters alone and discovers that the princess has transformed into an ogress.
She explains that during her childhood, she was cursed to transform into an ogress at night but retain her human form during the day.
She tells the donkey that only "true love's first kiss" will break the spell and allow her to "take love's true form".
Meanwhile, the ogre is about to confess his feelings to the princess, when he overhears the princess referring to herself as an "ugly beast".
Thinking that she is talking about him, the ogre angrily leaves and returns the next morning with the lord.
Confused and hurt by the ogre's abrupt hostility, the princess reluctantly accepts the lord's marriage proposal and requests that they be married that day before sunset.
The ogre dismisses the donkey and returns to his now vacated swamp, but quickly realizes that he feels miserable without the princess.

The donkey returns and lectures the ogre for jumping to conclusions and reveals that the princess was not referring to him as an "ugly beast", although the donkey does not reveal the princess's secret to the ogre.
The two reconcile, and the donkey summons the dragon, whom he had reunited with earlier in the day.
The ogre and the donkey ride the dragon to the kingdom so they can stop the wedding.
The ogre interrupts the ceremony just before it ends and expresses his feelings for the princess.
The sun sets, and the princess transforms into an ogress in front of everyone.
Disgusted and enraged, the lord orders the ogre to be executed and the princess re-imprisoned, while he declares himself king.
The two are saved when the dragon, ridden by the donkey, breaks in and devours the lord.
The ogre and the princess kiss, and the princess's curse is broken; though she remains an ogress, the ogre reassures her that he still finds her beautiful.
They marry in the swamp with the fairy tale creatures in attendance, then leave for their honeymoon.
A ten-year-old girl and her parents are traveling to their new home in the countryside.
They drive down an unexpected road and arrive in front of a tunnel leading to what appears to be an abandoned resort town, which her parents insist on exploring over the girl's protests.
Upon finding a seemingly empty restaurant stocked with food, the girl's parents begin to eat.
While exploring further, the girl finds an enormous bathhouse and meets a boy, who warns her to return across the riverbed before sunset.
Spirits begin to appear, and the girl discovers that her parents have been transformed into pigs and that she cannot cross the now-flooded river.
The boy finds the girl and tells her to ask for a job from the bathhouse's boiler-man, a yōkai spirit.
The boiler-man instead asks a worker to bring the girl to the boiler-man's master, the witch who runs the bathhouse and who transformed the girl's parents.
The witch tries to frighten the girl away but eventually gives her a work contract.
As the girl signs the contract with her name, the witch takes away the second kanji in her name, renaming her.

The girl soon forgets her real name, and the boy explains that the witch controls people by taking their names; if the girl completely forgets her name like the boy did, she will never be able to leave the spirit world.
Workers in the bathhouse mock the girl.
While working, she invites a silent creature inside, believing him to be a customer.
The spirit of a polluted river arrives as the girl's first customer.
After she cleans him, he gives her a magic emetic dumpling as a token of gratitude.
Meanwhile, the creature demands food from the bathhouse workers, giving them gold in exchange.
When the girl declines the gold and leaves to find the boy, the creature angrily swallows some workers.
The girl sees paper shikigami spirits attacking a dragon and recognizes the dragon as a metamorphosed boy.
When the seriously injured boy crashes into the witch's penthouse, the girl follows him upstairs.
A shikigami that stowed away on her back shapeshifts into the witch's twin sister, who turns the witch's son into a mouse and creates a false copy of him.
The twin sister tells the girl that the boy has stolen a magic golden seal from her that carries a deadly curse.
The boy strikes the shikigami, causing the twin sister to vanish.
The girl and the boy fall into the boiler room, where she feeds him part of the emetic dumpling, causing him to vomit up the seal and a slug, which the girl kills.
The girl resolves to return the seal and apologize to the twin sister.
She confronts the engorged creature and feeds him the rest of the dumpling, forcing him to regurgitate the workers.
The creature follows the girl out of the bathhouse, and the worker helps them leave.
The girl, the creature, and the witch's son travel to see the twin sister using train tickets from the boiler-man.
Meanwhile, the witch nearly orders the girl's parents slaughtered, but the boy reveals the witch's son is missing and offers to retrieve him if the witch releases the girl and her parents.
The twin sister reveals to the girl that the witch used the slug to control the boy.
The twin sister tells the girl that she cannot help her parents, but she makes her a magical protective hairband.
Using his dragon form, the boy flies the girl and the witch's son back, while the creature decides to stay with the twin sister.
Mid-flight, the girl recalls falling into a river years earlier and being washed safely ashore.
She correctly guesses the boy's true identity as the spirit of that river, which restores his memory.
When they arrive at the bathhouse, the witch tests the girl, asking her to identify her parents among a group of pigs.
After she answers correctly that none of the pigs are her parents, her contract disappears and she is given back her real name.
The boy takes her to the now-dry riverbed and vows to meet her again.
The girl crosses the riverbed to her restored parents.
Shortly before leaving for her new home, the girl looks back at the tunnel, still wearing her hairband from the twin sister.
The father and the mother live in a semi-basement flat (banjiha) in the city with their daughter and son.
As the family has financial struggles and low-income jobs, a family friend gives them a scholar's rock meant to promise wealth.
Leaving to study abroad, he suggests that the son lie about his qualifications to take over the friend's job as an English tutor for a girl, the daughter of a wealthy but naïve family.
The friend trusts the son because he likes the girl and wants to ask her out when he returns.

After the daughter helps forge a certificate for him, the son, posing as a university student under a false name, goes to the wealthy family's home, where he is hired by the wealthy mother by the end of his first lesson.
The poor family's scheme is to secure jobs for each family member within the wealthy household while concealing their true identities.

The son recommends someone with a false name, actually the daughter, as an art therapist for the wealthy family's young son, who has been traumatised from having a seizure after seeing a "ghost" in their kitchen.
The daughter then frames the wealthy family's chauffeur by making it appear as though he had a sexual encounter in the car, leading to the father being hired as his replacement.

The poor family exploit the peach allergy of the wealthy family's longtime housekeeper to convince the wealthy mother that the housekeeper has tuberculosis, and the mother is hired as her replacement.
Meanwhile, the son begins a secret romantic relationship with the girl.

While the wealthy family are away on a camping trip, the poor family revel in the luxuries of the house when the housekeeper suddenly appears at the door, claiming to have forgotten something in the basement.
She goes through a hidden entrance to an underground bunker created by the house's architect and previous owner, who had kept its existence secret from the wealthy family.
There, the housekeeper's husband has been hiding from loan sharks and is revealed to be the "ghost" the boy saw.

The housekeeper begs the mother to allow her husband to continue living there in exchange for regular payments, but the three other members of the poor family, who are eavesdropping, accidentally reveal their true identities.
The housekeeper films them and threatens to expose their deception to the wealthy family.

After the wealthy family call to inform the poor family that they are returning early due to a sudden severe rainstorm, the poor family quickly destroy all evidence of their ruse and subdue the housekeeper and her husband in the bunker, although the housekeeper is injured during the struggle.
The poor family manage to escape, but the torrential rain floods their flat with sewage water, forcing them to take shelter in a gymnasium alongside other displaced people.
The next day, the wealthy mother organises an impromptu garden party for the boy's birthday, with the father and the mother assisting while the son and the daughter are invited as guests.
The son enters the bunker with his scholar's rock, with intentions unknown.
The housekeeper is already dead from injuries sustained in the previous day's brawl; her husband bludgeons the son with the rock, leaving him unconscious.
The husband then leaves the bunker and stabs the daughter with a kitchen knife in front of horrified party guests.
The boy seizes upon seeing the "ghost" again.
The mother impales the husband with a barbecue skewer after a struggle.
While the father tends to the daughter, the wealthy father orders him to drive the boy to the hospital.
The father, gradually enraged by the wealthy family's lack of empathy or awareness of their own privilege, stabs him with the husband's knife and flees.
Weeks later, the son is recovering from brain surgery, and he and the mother have been convicted of fraud and placed on probation.
The daughter has died from her injuries, and the father – now a wanted fugitive – has disappeared.
The housekeeper's husband is presumed to have been a random homeless man, and the motives for the murders remain unsolved.
The son spies on the wealthy family's former home, now owned by a foreign family, and notices a coded message in a light visible from outside.
The father, hiding in the bunker, has buried the housekeeper in the garden and sends daily messages, hoping the son will see them.
Still living in a semi-basement flat with his mother, the son writes a letter to the father, vowing to earn enough money one day to buy the house and free him.
The family of a wealthy mystery novelist attends his birthday party at his estate.
The next morning, the novelist's housekeeper discovers him dead with a slit throat.
Police detectives believe the novelist died by suicide, but a private detective is anonymously hired to investigate the novelist's death.
The detective learns the novelist had strained relationships with his family members, giving several of them plausible motives for murder.
Unbeknownst to the detective, the novelist's nurse believes she injected the novelist with a lethal dose of morphine after mixing up his bedtime medications the night of the party.

To protect the nurse from being blamed for his death, the novelist instructed the nurse to create a false alibi before he slit his own throat: she was to be seen leaving the house, sneak back in through a window, and disguise herself as the novelist in order to make it appear that he was alive after she left for the night.
The nurse cannot lie without vomiting, so she gives accurate but incomplete answers when questioned.
She agrees to assist the detective's investigation and conceals evidence incriminating her.
At the reading of the novelist's will, the nurse is bequeathed his entire fortune and property, stunning the family.
The novelist's grandson helps the nurse flee but manipulates her into confessing to him.
The grandson offers further assistance in exchange for a portion of the nurse's inheritance.
Meanwhile, the other family members unsuccessfully attempt to influence the nurse to renounce the inheritance, even threatening to have her undocumented mother deported.
The nurse receives a blackmail note containing a partial photocopy of the novelist's toxicology report.
She and the grandson drive to the medical examiner's office, only to find it burned down.
The nurse receives an email proposing a meeting with the blackmailer; the detective and the police spot them, leading to the grandson being arrested.
At the meeting, the nurse finds that the housekeeper, the blackmailer, has been drugged; she performs CPR on the housekeeper and calls an ambulance.
The nurse confesses to the detective, but discovers the grandson has already implicated her.
Out of moral obligation, the nurse believes she must confess to the family, which would invalidate the bequest under the slayer rule.
At the mansion, the nurse finds the housekeeper's copy of the full toxicology report, which shows the novelist had only trace amounts of morphine in his blood.
The detective reveals his deductions to the police, the nurse, and the grandson.
The detective deduces the novelist told the grandson about his will, prompting the grandson to swap the novelist's medicines to cause the nurse to kill him unknowingly.

However, the nurse actually gave the novelist the correct medication, recognizing it by viscosity without reading the label due to her experience as a nurse; she only believed she had poisoned the novelist after reading the label on the bottle with the switched content.
When the death was reported as a suicide, the grandson anonymously hired the detective to entrap the nurse.
The housekeeper saw the grandson tampering with the crime scene to remove the switched medications, and sent him the blackmail note.

After the grandson realized that the nurse was not responsible for the novelist's death but believed she was, he forwarded the blackmail letter to the nurse and burned down the medical examiner's office to destroy evidence of her innocence.
The grandson then overdosed the housekeeper with morphine, intending for the nurse to be caught with the housekeeper's corpse.
The nurse receives a call from the hospital informing her that the housekeeper has died from her overdose.
Since there is no evidence of the grandson committing a murder, the nurse lies to the group that the housekeeper is alive while suppressing her urge to vomit.
This tricks the grandson into confirming his involvement with the housekeeper's overdose, inadvertently confessing to murder.
Realizing his loss, the grandson attacks the nurse with a knife from the novelist's collection but the knife is a harmless retractable stage knife.
The police promptly arrest him.
The detective tells the nurse he suspected early on that she played a part in the novelist's death, noting a drop of blood on her shoe.
He tells the nurse her innocence prevailed because she made ethical choices that obstructed the grandson's attempts to incriminate her.

As the grandson is taken into custody and the rest of the family is gathered outside in defeat, the nurse watches from the balcony of what is now her mansion, sipping from the novelist's coffee mug that reads "My House, My Rules, My Coffee!!".
On a suburban street at night, a Black man walks alone, talking on his phone.
After a car approaches him, the man, sensing trouble, attempts to escape, but is subdued, dragged into the car and driven away.
Six months later, a Black photographer travels upstate for a weekend getaway to meet the family of his white girlfriend.
Upon arrival, he has uncomfortable conversations with the girlfriend's father, a neurosurgeon, and mother, a psychiatrist.
Later, the girlfriend's brother arrives, and the photographer observes eerie behavior from the family's Black staff, a female staff member and a male staff member.
The psychiatrist manipulates the photographer into an individual hypnotherapy session, using the sound of a spoon stirring in a teacup as a hypnotic trigger, ostensibly to cure his smoking habit.
While entranced, he reveals that his mother died in a hit-and-run when he was 11 years old; he feels partially responsible, as he delayed calling for help.
At the psychiatrist's prompting, his consciousness falls into a dark void she dubs the "sunken place", where his body becomes temporarily paralyzed.
The next morning, he finds that he no longer has a desire to smoke.
Dozens of wealthy white guests arrive for the family's annual get-together and continually make uncomfortable remarks toward the photographer.
The photographer meets a blind art dealer, who takes an interest in his photography, and a Black man.
Like the male staff member and the female staff member, the man behaves unnaturally, and is married to a white woman thirty years his senior.
When the photographer photographs the man with flash on, the man lunges toward the photographer, frantically telling him to "get out."
The neurosurgeon removes him, later explaining the sudden erratic behavior as a seizure.
The photographer confides in the girlfriend about his worries, and both ultimately agree to return home.
Meanwhile, as the party guests have a silent auction for a photo of him, the photographer sends the photo of the man to his friend, an airport security officer.
The friend recognizes the man as a missing man from the city.

The photographer discovers photos of the girlfriend dating numerous Black individuals, including the male staff member and the female staff member, and he tries to leave, but the brother and the neurosurgeon block the doors.
The girlfriend, revealing herself as an accomplice, refuses to give him his keys, and the psychiatrist hypnotizes him back to the sunken place.

Awakening strapped to an armchair in the basement, the photographer views a video in which the neurosurgeon's father explains that the family transplants the brains of wealthy white people into Black bodies to acquire their physical characteristics, leaving the host's consciousness trapped in the "sunken place".

The art dealer then reveals that he is going to be transferred into the photographer's body, but maintains that he does not care about the color of the photographer's skin and only covets a body with working eyesight.
Meanwhile, the friend consults the police, who laugh off his theory about the family.
In another room, the neurosurgeon begins the transplantation process, removing the top of the art dealer's skull.

The brother arrives to retrieve the photographer, who has seemingly been hypnotized by a clip of the teacup sound earlier, but the photographer awakens and bludgeons him—having blocked the trigger by plugging his ears with cotton stuffing from the armchair.
The photographer kills the neurosurgeon, who sets the operating room ablaze, then the psychiatrist, then the brother when he attacks again.
Attempting to escape in the brother's car, the photographer accidentally hits the female staff member, who possesses the brain of the girlfriend's grandmother.
Reminded of his own mother's death, the photographer guiltily takes her into the car, but she reawakens and attacks him, causing the car to crash and kill her.
The girlfriend and the male staff member, who possesses the grandfather's brain, arrive to capture the photographer.
During a scuffle, the photographer uses his phone's flash to free the male staff member from the grandfather's control.
The male staff member shoots the girlfriend with her rifle, then fatally shoots himself.
The photographer begins strangling the girlfriend, but relents when she manipulatively pleads for her life and promises she loves him.
A police car arrives; the girlfriend cries out for help, but the friend emerges from the car and picks up the photographer, leaving the girlfriend to bleed out on the road.
